# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy for Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a major cause of morbidity, mortality, and healthcare expenditure worldwide, affecting more than 64 million people globally [1]. Despite advances in guideline-directed medical therapy and device-based interventions such as cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), a substantial proportion of patients remain symptomatic [2]. Importantly, only about one-third of patients with HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) meet criteria for CRT, owing to the requirement for a wide QRS complex [3]. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) therapy has emerged as a device-based option for patients with narrow QRS who remain symptomatic despite optimal therapy [4].

## Mechanism of Action

CCM delivers non-excitatory electrical signals to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period of the cardiac cycle [5]. Because these signals are timed to occur after local depolarization, they do not initiate a new action potential but instead modulate myocardial contractility [6]. Experimental studies demonstrate that CCM enhances calcium handling, increasing the magnitude of intracellular calcium transients and improving contractile force [7]. At the molecular level, CCM appears to reverse aspects of the maladaptive fetal gene program, normalizing expression of key calcium-cycling proteins such as SERCA2a, phospholamban, and ryanodine receptors [8]. These effects suggest a degree of reverse remodeling rather than merely acute inotropy [9].

## Clinical Evidence

The clinical development of CCM has progressed through several randomized trials. The FIX-HF-4 study, a European double-blind crossover trial, demonstrated improvements in peak oxygen consumption (VO2) and quality of life with CCM, though a placebo effect complicated interpretation [10]. The FIX-HF-5 trial enrolled patients with NYHA class III–IV symptoms and ejection fraction ≤35%; while the primary composite endpoint of ventilatory anaerobic threshold was not met, prespecified subgroup analyses suggested benefit in patients with ejection fraction between 25% and 45% [11]. This finding informed the design of the subsequent FIX-HF-5C study [12].

FIX-HF-5C confirmed that, in patients with ejection fraction 25–45%, CCM significantly improved peak VO2, six-minute walk distance, and quality of life as measured by the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire [12]. A pooled analysis incorporating FIX-HF-5C and related cohorts further supported improvements in exercise tolerance and a possible reduction in HF hospitalizations [13]. On the basis of these data, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration granted approval for the Optimizer device in 2019 [14].

Long-term registries and observational studies have reinforced the safety profile and sustained symptomatic benefit of CCM [15]. The CCM-REG registry demonstrated improvements in NYHA functional class and quality of life maintained over two years, with mortality rates lower than predicted by the Seattle Heart Failure Model [16]. Real-world European data have also reported reductions in HF hospitalization rates following implantation [17].

## Patient Selection and Implantation

Current indications focus on symptomatic HFrEF patients (NYHA class III) with ejection fraction between 25% and 45%, normal QRS duration (<130 ms), and who remain symptomatic despite optimal medical therapy [18]. The Optimizer system is implanted similarly to a pacemaker, with leads placed on the right ventricular septum [19]. Notably, the device delivers therapy for several hours per day rather than continuously [20]. Procedural complication rates are comparable to those of conventional device implantation [21].

## Emerging Applications and Future Directions

Interest has grown in extending CCM to patients with HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), given the limited therapeutic options in this population [22]. Preliminary studies suggest possible symptomatic benefit, and dedicated trials are ongoing [23]. There is also increasing exploration of CCM in patients with atrial fibrillation, who were initially excluded from pivotal trials [24]. Combination with other devices, including implantable cardioverter-defibrillators, has been evaluated for feasibility and safety [25].

Mechanistic research continues to clarify CCM's effects on autonomic function, with evidence suggesting favorable modulation of sympathovagal balance [26]. Cost-effectiveness analyses have generally supported CCM as a reasonable use of resources within healthcare systems [27]. Nonetheless, important questions remain regarding its effect on hard endpoints such as mortality, and adequately powered outcome trials are needed [28]. The ongoing integration of CCM into HF management algorithms reflects a broader shift toward individualized device therapy [29]. Future studies leveraging remote monitoring and biomarker-guided optimization may further refine patient selection and improve outcomes [30].

## Conclusion

CCM therapy represents a valuable addition to the device-based management of symptomatic HFrEF patients with narrow QRS complexes who are ineligible for CRT. Robust evidence supports improvements in exercise capacity and quality of life, while emerging data explore broader applications including HFpEF. Definitive trials assessing mortality and hospitalization outcomes will determine its ultimate place in HF therapeutics.
